checks.claim: Key: a red dwarf's habitable zone lies much closer to it than Earth is to the Sun
checks.note: Grokipedia: late M dwarfs compress the zone to about 0.02-0.05 AU; NASA: red dwarfs have much tighter zones.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: about as far as Earth; much farther; nowhere (a dim star cannot warm a planet)
checks.note: All false: dimmer stars have zones closer in; even the very dim TRAPPIST-1 has planets in its zone.

checks.claim: Habitable zone defined as the distances where a planet's surface could keep liquid water
TRAPPIST-1 is a red dwarf with three planets in its habitable zone (e, f, g)
checks.note: NASA 2017: three of the seven (e, f, g) lie in the habitable zone. Grokipedia agrees (M8V ultracool red dwarf).

checks.claim: All three orbit far closer to their star than Mercury does to the Sun
checks.note: e, f, g at 0.029, 0.038, 0.047 AU vs Mercury 0.39 AU; NASA: all seven orbits are closer than Mercury's.

checks.claim: Earth sits inside the Sun's habitable zone; Venus lies inside its inner edge
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Venus, at 0.72 AU, lies inside the inner HZ edge'; Earth 'firmly within this zone at 1 AU'.

checks.claim: Key: the Moon's gravity is too weak to hold gas
checks.note: Grokipedia attributes the lack of air mainly to weak gravity (escape velocity 2.38 km/s vs 11.2 km/s), with solar-wind stripping as a further loss.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Earth's gravity pulls its gas away
checks.note: Earth's influence is only small tidal and magnetotail effects; not why the Moon lacks air.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it has no ozone layer to seal air in
checks.note: Ozone absorbs UV; it does not hold an atmosphere in.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it spins too slowly to keep air
checks.note: Spin is not a retention factor (slow-spinning Venus keeps thick air).

checks.claim: The Moon gets about as much sunlight as Earth; it has almost no air
Stem: 'any water left on its surface soon escapes into space'
checks.note: Overstated: NASA says most water on the Moon would be quickly vaporized by sunlight and lost, but some ends up in permanently shadowed polar craters, where ice is 'relatively stable' and accumulates in cold traps (the water Artemis is aiming for). Fix: 'and most water left on its sunlit surface soon escapes into space' (or 'water left in sunlight on its surface').

checks.claim: Context: escape speed about 2.4 km/s for the Moon, about 11.2 km/s for Earth
Context: some molecules of any gas move fast enough to escape a weak pull; any early air leaked away
checks.note: CK-12: a few molecules always move fast enough to escape; for the Moon any atmosphere would be lost within geological time.

checks.claim: Earth's average surface temperature about 15 C
checks.note: NASA: 'the comfortable 15C (59F) that it is today'.

checks.claim: Key: without greenhouse gases about -18 C
checks.note: NASA: 'a very chilly -18C (0F)'; Grokipedia Greenhouse_effect agrees (-18 C vs 15 C, about 33 C warming). The standard figure assumes today's reflectivity, consistent with 'the Sun shone just as before'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: -60 C, 5 C, 14 C
checks.note: None matches the standard result. (About 5 C is what a perfectly black, non-reflecting Earth would reach, which is not the stem's situation.)

checks.claim: Context: some 33 degrees colder; below freezing; greenhouse gases only a small part of the air
checks.note: Nitrogen and oxygen (78% and 21%) are not greenhouse gases.

checks.claim: Context: about -60 C is the average on Mars
checks.note: NASA fact sheet: about 214 K (-59 C); Grokipedia Atmosphere_of_Mars about -60 C. Other sources give -55 to -63 C; 'about -60' is fine.

checks.claim: No climate-change or policy content
checks.note: Natural greenhouse effect only.

checks.claim: Key: greenhouse gases absorb much of the rising infrared and send part back down
checks.note: NASA: 'much of it is absorbed by water vapor and long-lived greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane'; they 'radiate in all directions'; energy radiating back toward Earth heats the surface. Grokipedia: re-emit in all directions, including downward.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: reflect all like a mirror; let all pass; trap all so none leaves
checks.note: All false: absorption and re-emission, not reflection; Earth still radiates energy to space.

checks.claim: Stem: sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground; the ground gives off infrared, invisible to human eyes; water vapour and CO2 are greenhouse gases
Context: nitrogen and oxygen, nearly all the air, let infrared pass straight through
checks.note: Grokipedia: nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) are 'transparent to infrared'.

checks.claim: Stem: early rocks show the air held almost no free oxygen
checks.note: Below 10^-6 of present levels; sulfur-isotope (MIF) evidence in older rocks.

checks.claim: Stem: oxygen is about a fifth of the air today
checks.note: About 21%.

checks.claim: Key: most of the oxygen came from microbes that made food from sunlight
checks.note: Cyanobacteria started the oxygen and are the right answer among these four choices, but 'most' is shaky: after the Great Oxidation Event oxygen sat near 1-10% of today's level for a very long time, land plants are credited with the later rise toward today's 21% (about 350 million years ago), and today about half of the oxygen made each year comes from ocean plankton and half from land plants. Fix: key 'Living things that made food from sunlight' (plants included), or reword the stem to 'What first filled the air with oxygen?'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: volcanoes; comets; rocks giving it off as they weathered
checks.note: Volcanic gas is mostly water vapour, CO2 and SO2 (over 99%), no free O2 listed; weathering consumes oxygen rather than releasing it; comets are not the source.

checks.claim: Context: cyanobacteria, photosynthesising microbes, began filling the air with oxygen about 2.4 billion years ago, the Great Oxidation Event
checks.note: Onset about 2.43 Ga (span about 2.45-2.32 Ga); 'the primary driver of the GOE was the advent and proliferation of cyanobacteria'.

checks.claim: Context: 'At first the oxygen joined with iron dissolved in the sea, and only later did it build up in the air'
checks.note: True, but placed after '2.4 billion years ago' it reads as if the iron sink came after the GOE. Grokipedia: oxygen was consumed by dissolved iron until that supply ran out around 2.4 Ga, then built up. Suggested order: 'Cyanobacteria ... made oxygen; at first it joined with iron dissolved in the sea, and only about 2.4 billion years ago did it begin to build up in the air, in what is called the Great Oxidation Event.'

checks.claim: Context: volcanic gas is mostly water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, not oxygen
Stem: most ozone lies about 15 to 35 km up, in the stratosphere
checks.note: Grokipedia: about 15 to 35 km, about 90% of ozone in this layer. EPA gives 15-30 km (main text) and 15-40 km (glossary).

checks.claim: Key: sunburn from the Sun's ultraviolet light
checks.note: Thinner ozone lets more UV-B through; UV-B causes sunburn, skin cancers, cataracts.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: heatstroke from hotter air near the ground
checks.note: NASA: the extra UV 'cannot explain the warming of the planet's surface'; net effect cools the stratosphere.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: shortness of breath from air low in oxygen
checks.note: Breathed O2 is in the lower air; ozone is a trace gas.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: harm from the Sun's charged particles
checks.note: Charged particles are turned aside by the magnetic field, not the ozone layer.

checks.claim: Context: 'The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet light'
checks.note: False as written: EPA says 'UVA is not absorbed by ozone' (Grokipedia: negligible UV-A absorption), and UV-A is the largest share of the Sun's ultraviolet; ozone absorbs all UV-C and most UV-B, i.e. 97-99% of the HARMFUL UV. Fix: 'The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light, which burns skin...'

checks.claim: Context: extra UV does not make the air noticeably hotter; breathed oxygen is in the lower air
Context: the Antarctic ozone hole was reported in 1985
checks.note: May 1985, British Antarctic Survey (Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin), Halley station.

checks.claim: Stem: molten iron churning in the outer core makes Earth's magnetic field, reaching far into space
checks.note: Geodynamo: convecting, electrically conducting molten iron alloy in the outer core.

checks.claim: Key: with no field, the solar wind would strike the top of the air far more
checks.note: The magnetosphere 'deflects most incoming plasma'; with no field the solar wind would meet the upper atmosphere directly (as at Venus and Mars). The question asks only what would strike the air, not whether air would be lost, so it stays clear of the debate over how much a magnetic field matters for keeping an atmosphere.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: ultraviolet, infrared, visible light
checks.note: Light (photons) carries no charge and is not deflected by a magnetic field; its arrival would not change.

checks.claim: Context: solar wind is charged particles; the field steers most around the planet; a few are guided toward the poles and make auroras
checks.note: Grokipedia: charged particles 'guided by Earth's magnetic field lines toward polar regions'; particle precipitation drives auroras.

checks.claim: Context: 'Ultraviolet light is held back by the ozone layer instead'
checks.note: Acceptable as a statement of which shield acts on UV, but ozone stops UV-C and most UV-B, not UV-A. Optional tweak for consistency with the ozone question: 'Most harmful ultraviolet light is held back by the ozone layer instead.'

checks.claim: Stem: Mars lost its global magnetic field about 4 billion years ago
checks.note: Grokipedia: dynamo 'ceased around 4 billion years ago'; timeline section 4.0-3.9 Ga; some newer evidence of weak dynamo activity to about 3.7 Ga. 'About 4 billion years ago' covers the usual estimates; if a later source pushes the date, 'billions of years ago' would be the safe wording.

checks.claim: Stem: a NASA spacecraft (MAVEN) began orbiting Mars in 2014 to study how the solar wind strikes the upper air
checks.note: MAVEN entered Mars orbit 21 September 2014 (launched November 2013 per NASA).

checks.claim: Key: the team found the solar wind stripped much of Mars's air into space
checks.note: NASA 2015: solar wind 'strips away gas'; loss 'likely a major process in changing the Martian climate'. LASP 2017: majority of Mars's CO2 lost to space by sputtering.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: boiled its seas with the Sun's heat; blew its dust into planet-wide storms; turned its rocks red with rust
checks.note: None is a MAVEN finding about the solar wind. Mars is red from iron oxide, but that is not what the solar wind did or what the team reported.

checks.claim: Context: about 100 grams a second today, likely far more when the young Sun was stormier
checks.note: 'about 100 grams (roughly 1/4 pound) every second'; 'the loss rate was much higher billions of years ago when the sun was young and more active'.

checks.claim: Context: in 2017 the team reported most of Mars's air had been lost this way
checks.note: About 65% of argon lost by sputtering; Jakosky: 'the majority of the planet's CO2 was also lost to space by sputtering' (a minimum).

checks.claim: Context: with no global field the solar wind knocks gas off the top of Mars's air
checks.note: Describes the mechanism at Mars (ion pickup, sputtering); it does not claim a field would have saved the air, so the open debate is not overstated.

checks.claim: Context: dry riverbeds show water once flowed; Mars is now a frigid desert
checks.note: LASP 2017: 'into a frigid desert world'; Mariner 9 and later missions imaged dry riverbeds (National Geographic 2019).

checks.claim: Stem: Venus and Mars both have air made mostly of CO2
checks.note: Venus 96.5%, Mars 95.1% (NASA fact sheets).

checks.claim: Stem: on Venus the gas warms the ground by hundreds of degrees; on Mars hardly at all
checks.note: Venus greenhouse about 462 C (Grokipedia: over 500 K); Mars 'essentially negligible'.

checks.claim: Key: Venus's air holds vastly more of the gas
checks.note: OpenStax: 'the venusian atmosphere is more than 10,000 times more massive than its martian counterpart'; NASA fact sheets 4.8e20 kg vs 2.5e16 kg (about 19,000 times).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Venus's clouds let all of the sunlight through
checks.note: Bond albedo 0.77.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Mars's CO2 is too cold to trap heat
checks.note: The difference is the amount of gas (thin air), not its temperature.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Venus spins so slowly its long days bake it
checks.note: Diurnal temperature range about 0: nights as hot as days.

checks.claim: Context: clouds reflect about three-quarters of the sunlight; nights as hot as days; 'runaway greenhouse'
checks.note: Albedo 0.77 (NASA), Grokipedia 75%; OpenStax names the runaway greenhouse effect. The context does not claim Venus had oceans, so the open question about early Venusian oceans is avoided.

checks.claim: Stem: Venus's air is about 96 percent CO2; Earth's holds only a trace
checks.note: 96.5% by volume; Earth about 0.04%.

checks.claim: Key: most of Earth's CO2 is locked up in rocks such as limestone
checks.note: NASA: most of Earth's carbon is stored in rocks; shells and sediment become limestone. BGS: over 99% of the carbon in the carbon cycle is in the crust.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: bodies of living things; carried off by solar wind; frozen in polar ice
checks.note: Living things hold a tiny share next to rock; Earth's polar ice is water ice, not CO2; solar-wind loss of CO2 is not where Earth's went.

checks.claim: Context: rain dissolves CO2, wears down rock, rivers carry it to the sea, where it settles as carbonate rock
checks.note: The carbonate-silicate cycle, simplified (in the sea much of the carbonate is built into shells first); still true at grade level.

checks.claim: Context: Earth's carbonate rocks hold about as much CO2 as Venus's whole atmosphere
checks.note: Review: Earth 'contains a similar amount of CO2 locked in carbonate rocks as exists in the Venusian atmosphere today'; textbook comparison, accurate within a factor of about two.

checks.claim: Context: Venus has no liquid water, so its CO2 stays in the air
checks.note: Grokipedia: without liquid water to weather CO2 into carbonates, outgassed CO2 built up.

unit_notes: No climate-change or policy content anywhere in the unit; the greenhouse questions keep to the natural effect. The magnetic-field questions are safe: one asks only what would strike the upper air, the other reports MAVEN's attributed finding; neither claims a field is what keeps an atmosphere. Two fixes needed: the Moon stem's 'any water left on its surface soon escapes' (polar cold traps keep ice) and the ozone context's 'absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet light' (UV-A passes; say 'harmful'). The oxygen question's key says 'most' of the oxygen came from microbes; land plants also raised oxygen to today's level, so 'Living things that made food from sunlight' would be safe.
